item.title: The scam text test: Spot danger before you tap
item.description: A simple six-step scam text test helps you spot phishing messages about fake deliveries, toll notices and bank alerts before you click or share anything.
item.content:encoded:
Your phone buzzes. The text reads, "Your package is delayed. Confirm your address here." A little later, it's a text message about an unpaid toll, suspicious bank activity or an account that will be locked unless you act now.

That's how scam texts work. They don't always look wild or obviously fake. They look routine, urgent and easy to deal with in a hurry. The good news: You don't need to memorize every scam. You just need a quick way to test suspicious messages before you tap. Here's the simple scam text test to run before you click, pay or share anything.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA

If a text asks you to click, pay, verify, sign in or fix a problem, run through these checks first.

Are you actually waiting for that package? Do you use that bank? Did you recently drive on a toll road? If the answer is no, treat the message as suspicious. Even if the answer is yes, don't assume it's real. Scammers rely on coincidence. They send thousands of similar messages knowing that some recipients will be waiting for a package or use the company being impersonated.

Urgency is one of the biggest red flags. Watch for phrases like:

A real company may send an urgent alert, but scammers use pressure to stop you from checking whether the message is legitimate. Take a breath before responding. A few extra minutes spent verifying the message can prevent days or weeks of dealing with a stolen account.

Before tapping, check for:

Even if the address looks legitimate, avoid opening links in unexpected texts. Scammers can disguise links or create convincing copies of real websites. Verify the message through the company's official app or a website you type in yourself.

Many scam texts use vague greetings, odd wording, awkward punctuation or slightly incorrect brand names. You might see a message addressed to "Dear customer" instead of your name. It may refer to a package without showing an order number or claim to come from a bank without identifying the account involved. Good grammar doesn't guarantee a message is safe. Scammers now use artificial intelligence to write more convincing messages. Still, sloppy wording and missing details remain warning signs.

Be skeptical of any text asking for:

Legitimate companies may send you a one-time verification code. However, a bank, government agency or customer service representative should never ask you to give that code to someone else. Anyone who asks for your code may be trying to take control of your account.

This is the most important step. Instead of using the link or phone number in the message:

If the issue is real, you should still be able to find it through one of those trusted channels.

FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK

Scam texts often fall into a few familiar categories.

These messages claim a package was delayed, an address needs to be corrected or a small shipping fee must be paid. The link may lead to afake postal or delivery websitethat collects your card information, password or home address.

These texts claim someone used your card, your account has been locked or you must verify a transaction immediately. The message may include a phone number connecting you to a scammer pretending to work for the bank.

Toll scams claim you owe a small amount and will face a larger penalty if you don't pay immediately. The amount is often low enough to make paying seem easier than investigating. The payment page then steals your financial information.

These messages claim your email, payment app, streaming service or social media account will be suspended. They direct you to a fake login page designed to capture your username and password. These scams work because each message sounds plausible. The goal is to make you react first and think later.

Don't panic, but act quickly.

Simply opening a phishing page doesn't always mean your information was stolen. The risk increases if you entered information, downloaded a file or approved a permission request.

Use a different password for every important account. A password manager can create and store strong passwords so one stolen login doesn't give scammers access to everything else.

Change the affected account's password immediately and check whether a new device, email address or phone number was added. Contact the company through its official app, website or phone number. Tell the representative that someone may have gained access to your account.

Report any charges you don't recognize as soon as possible.

HOTEL WI-FI PHISHING ATTACK TARGETS MICROSOFT LOGINS

Visit IdentityTheft.gov to create a recovery plan. You may also want to place a fraud alert or security freeze on your credit files. A credit freeze can prevent criminals from opening many types of new accounts in your name.

Avoid entering sensitive information on the device until you are confident it is secure.

After securing your accounts:

Reporting scam texts helps phone carriers and government agencies identify active campaigns.

Good habits are your first line of defense, but strong antivirus software can add another layer of protection. Some security tools can warn you about suspicious links, phishing websites and malicious downloads before they put your information at risk.

Many text scams are only the first step. The message sends you to a fake website. That site may steal your password, payment details or other personal information. In some cases, it may also try to install malware on your device.

Look for security software that offers:

Security software cannot catch every scam or replace careful judgment. Still, it can help stop a suspicious link or malicious download before one quick tap leads to fraud or an account takeover. Features vary by provider and device, so check what is included before choosing a service.

Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

You never have to solve a surprise text from inside the text. Stop, verify independently and only act through official channels. That one habit can help you avoid a huge number of text scams.

Scam texts work because they make an everyday problem feel urgent. A package delay, unpaid toll or bank warning can seem believable enough to make you tap without thinking. Don't use the link or phone number in the message. Open the company's official app, type its website yourself or call a number you already trust. Strong antivirus software can help flag some suspicious texts and fake websites, but no security tool catches everything. Taking a few seconds to verify the message can save you from a stolen account or a costly mistake.

item.title: Jelly Roll says he's planning to 'take some time off and heal' after final tour stop
item.description: Jelly Roll told fans he's taking a year or two off to "heal" after finalizing his divorce from Bunnie Xo and wrapping his tour with Post Malone.
item.content:encoded:
Jelly Roll announced that he is taking an indefinite hiatus from touring following a tumultuous year in his personal life.

While performing at the Rice-Eccles Stadium in Salt Lake City, Utah, on July 28, the 41-year-old country star, who recently finalized his divorce from his ex-wife Bunnie Xo, 46, revealed that he would not be hitting the road again for the foreseeable future.

"This has truly been a lifetime experience for me," the "Save Me" singer told the crowd, via Country Now. "And in a couple of nights, I go to Colorado Springs and do my last show for a year or two. I’m fixing to take some time off and heal. Thank you for the opportunity."

KACEY MUSGRAVES ABRUPTLY CANCELS CONCERT DATES FROM 'MIDDLE OF NOWHERE' TOUR

Fox News Digital has reached out to Jelly Roll's representatives for comment. 

The July 28 concert in Salt Lake City marked the final stop on Jelly Roll and Post Malone's co-headlining "BIG ASS Stadium Tour Part 2." Jelly Roll gave his final scheduled performance at his solo show at Weidner Field in Colorado Springs, Colorado, on July 30. Per Jelly Roll's official website, the rapper has no upcoming concert dates.

Jelly Roll's break from touring comes after he and Bunnie split following almost 10 years of marriage. The two first met in 2015 at a concert in Las Vegas and they eloped a year later. Following their marriage, she became a stepmother to the country singer’s daughter, Bailee, and son, Noah.

The "Son of a Sinner" hitmaker filed for divorce from Bunnie on May 18, but he listed the date of separation as May 9. Jelly Roll, whose real name is James DeBoard, cited "irreconcilable differences" as the reason for the split. The former couple finalized their divorce in early July.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

JELLY ROLL FILES FOR DIVORCE FROM WIFE BUNNIE XO AFTER ALMOST A DECADE OF MARRIAGE

Terms of their settlement remain confidential. However, People reported at the time that the former couple would split their assets, including homes, cars, an aircraft and any intellectual property.

Additionally, Jelly Roll would make a "one-time, confidential lump sum payment to Bunnie, so there will be no alimony claims to be made in court," the outlet reported.

Jelly Roll previously shut down speculation that infidelity led to the split, telling fans "nobody cheated on nobody," a claim later echoed by his daughter Bailee. Bunnie also denied that either she or Jelly Roll were unfaithful, saying on her "Dumb Blonde" podcast that "nobody cheated."

Last month, Bunnie made headlines after she was seen kissing reality TV personality Dylan Wolf at Jelly Roll's Goodnight Nashville Bar over the Fourth of July weekend. She later said on her podcast that she wasn't dating the "Calabasas Confidential" star, describing the PDA as part of her "hot girl summer" and adding that Jelly Roll "gets it."

In a since-deleted June podcast episode, Bunnie claimed that Jelly Roll had "started dating" again after their split.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Since the split, Jelly Roll has remained focused on his career, releasing the inspirational single "Hands Up" in June. The country star, who has lost 275 pounds over the last few years, has also continued to chronicle nearly every step of his health journey, celebrating both major milestones and the everyday habits that have fueled his transformation.

Despite untangling their finances and going their separate ways, Jelly Roll and Bunnie have made it clear they aren't severing every tie.

She said on a since-deleted episode of her podcast that the former couple still plans to have a baby via surrogate and co-parent after their divorce, and Jelly Roll later told fans that "every word" of her podcast was "the truth" while calling her his "best friend."

item.title: Paul Finebaum’s proclamation about Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer reignites college football ‘culture fit’ debate
item.description: Paul Finebaum says Kalen DeBoer lacks the right ingredients to win a national championship at Alabama despite averaging top-three recruiting classes.
item.content:encoded:
I mentioned it a while back, but August is the only time of year when almost every college football fanbase feels like their team has a chance to win it all.

Hope does indeed spring eternal every summer, but there are still plenty of programs who realistically have no shot at even making a College Football Playoff appearance.

One juggernaut who has historically been among the "haves" rather than the "have nots" is the Alabama Crimson Tide, but according to college football commentator Paul Finebaum, Bama's days of owning the lion's share of championship trophies may have come to an abrupt halt.

And it's all thanks to the man they hired to fill the team-issued polo previously worn by Nick Saban.

DID ALABAMA DOOM THEMSELVES TO MEDIOCRITY WITH KALEN DEBOER EXTENSION?

"I'm selling that," Finebaum said on Crane & Co. when asked if he would "buy or sell" Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer winning a natty while in Tuscaloosa. "I'll spare you the 'I think Kalen DeBoer is a good football coach.' I think everybody does. The question is, 'is he going to win a championship at Alabama?' And my answer is no."

Finebaum goes on to call the "culture fit" between DeBoer and Bama "okay," and says Alabama is a unique job where sometimes really good football coaches don't necessarily win titles due to factors that go far beyond the painted lines of Bryant Denny Stadium.

"In the last 60 years, only three people have won national championships, two of them happen to be the greatest coach of all-time on the day they retired," Finebaum stated. "At Alabama, you can be unique, you can be different, but Kalen DeBoer, to me, just doesn't have the right ingredients to win the title there."

'HOT SEAT RANKINGS' FOR ALL 16 SEC COACHES AS BEGINNING OF 2026 COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON DRAWS NEARER

It's interesting to hear Finebaum say that DeBoer doesn't have the right "ingredients" to win at Bama, but if you know what he means by that, it makes a ton of sense.

"Ingredients," in this instance, doesn't refer to talent on the field, because DeBoer and his staff haven't exactly been lacking in that department.

In the three full offseasons that DeBoer has been the head coach at Alabama, his average recruiting class ranking according to the 247Sports composite has been 2.5.

Every coach in America can only dream of averaging a top-three recruiting class every year they've been at their current school, but it's more than just a talent issue.

IF YOU BELIEVE ALABAMA WASN'T RECRUITING JEREMIAH SMITH, YOU DON'T UNDERSTAND RECRUITING

As Finebaum mentioned, the "culture fit" wasn't right from the start between DeBoer and his current employer, and though that may sound like a nebulous excuse, there's some real weight behind it.

"He's capable of winning it elsewhere," Finebaum reasoned. "He came within a reasonable chance of winning it at Washington. I think he could probably have won one at Michigan. Alabama's different."

For those who don't remember, DeBoer was rolling while coaching the Washington Huskies.

In his two seasons in the Pacific Northwest, DeBoer had two top-ten finishes and a national championship appearance under his belt.

BY ADDING ED ORGERON TO STAFF, LANE KIFFIN AND LSU ADDRESS KEY FLAW FROM PREVIOUS REGIME

Even before he arrived at the ranks of the Power 4, DeBoer was a noted winner, capturing three NAIA National Championships while at Sioux Falls and guiding Fresno State to a nine-win regular season in just his second year there.

The point is, DeBoer didn't just forget how to coach the moment his plane touched down in Tuscaloosa, and it's not like he's been an abject failure for the Tide either.

Averaging ten wins a year and making a CFP appearance would be welcomed at 99% of schools in the country.

But as Finebaum said so poignantly, "Alabama is different."

CURT CIGNETTI REVEALS HOW WORKING FOR NICK SABAN CHANGED EVERYTHING: 'EVERY DAY WAS 4TH-AND-1'

It's the same reason a guy like Brian Kelly, a coach who went 145-61 in his three FBS stops prior to landing in Baton Rouge, "failed" at LSU.

Kelly is not a bad coach or even an average coach, but he didn't understand the culture and expectations that come with being the Tigers' head coach.

Will DeBoer prove everyone wrong and win a title at Bama? I can't say for sure.

As long as they keep recruiting at their current pace, a coach like DeBoer has a chance.

WHAT DOES A REALISTICALLY SUCCESSFUL FIRST YEAR LOOK LIKE FOR HEAD COACH LANE KIFFIN AT LSU?

But I also wouldn't be shocked to see him looking for a job in two to three years either.

Programs like Alabama and LSU have one goal and one goal only: to win a national championship.

And sometimes, even that isn't enough to save your job (see: Ed Orgeron).

DeBoer will be judged by the trophy case he assembles while coaching the Crimson Tide, and right now, that sucker is looking a little empty.

item.title: Kelly Osbourne demands child support and her dogs back in fiery rant amid reported breakup
item.description: The since-deleted posts escalate from cryptic accusations to demands for child support and possessions amid her reported split from Sid Wilson.
item.content:encoded:
Kelly Osbourne appeared to take aim at her reported ex-fiancé, Sid Wilson.

The television personality sparked new questions about their relationship after posting a barrage of blistering Instagram Stories on Monday.

The since-deleted posts, viewed by Fox News Digital, appeared to accuse the musician of dodging accountability while vowing to put their son first.

KELLY OSBOURNE WELCOMES FIRST BABY WITH SID WILSON, SHARON OSBOURNE PRAISES DAUGHTER: 'SO PROUD'

Although Osbourne, 41, never mentioned Wilson by name, the timing and tone of the posts quickly raised questions about the pair's reported split.

One of her first messages took aim at someone she suggested was deflecting blame instead of accepting responsibility.

"Strange how the loudest defense of the guilty is rarely innocence... It's distraction. When the mask slips, they don't face the mirror they throw it at someone else. I also heard that when you break a mirror you get 7 years bad luck! Or is that just karma? This is why I always take accountability! As they say some are sicker then [sic] others," the post read.

Osbourne also reposted a quote that read, "My son's little heart once beat right beside mine. So trust me when I say... I will protect it at all costs," seemingly referring to the couple's 3-year-old son, Sidney.

In another message, she wrote, "Wake the f--- up and take some responsibility. I will not take your s--- anymore! I'm done. I want to be happy, and I have a beautiful son to raise. Leave me alone. Let me heal. I can't protect you from yourself anymore."

She later reposted another message about choosing children's well-being over everyone else's.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"My job is to protect my kids. Not your feelings. Not your expectations. Not judgments I didn't ask for. My responsibility is to protect their well-being. Their nervous systems. Their emotional safety. I will choose them every single time. Over anyone. Over anything."

Osbourne then appeared to reference unresolved issues involving possessions, finances and the care of their son.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"Also while I’m at it can I have my dogs back and all my possessions. Oh yeah and maybe some child support?"

Fox News Digital has reached out to Osbourne and Wilson for comment.

The cryptic posts add another chapter to the couple's reported breakup.

Osbourne and Wilson reportedly ended their engagement in March, about eight months after Wilson proposed, though neither has publicly confirmed the split.

The pair began dating in 2022 and welcomed their son, Sidney, later that year.

Meanwhile, Wilson has also faced career uncertainty in recent days.

SLIPKNOT’S SID WILSON SUFFERS SEVERE BURNS AFTER FARM EXPLOSION

The rocker was reportedly just fired from Slipknot after 28 years with the band, according to TMZ. The outlet reported the band had become fed up with Wilson's alleged behavior, particularly his treatment of fellow members.

Amid the speculation, Slipknot guitarist Jim Root urged fans not to jump to conclusions.

"Don’t believe everything you read," he wrote. "Stop. Think. Take a breath. Sit with it for awhile. Maybe. Just maybe even wait until there’s more information," according to People.

Wilson has not publicly addressed the reported firing.

item.title: David Ellison breaks silence on Paramount-WBD merger fight, CNN insiders don’t buy ‘lip service’ about network
item.description: Paramount CEO David Ellison says the real fight over his $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger is whether he can be trusted as a steward of CNN news.
item.content:encoded:
Paramount CEO David Ellison believes that opposition to his planned Warner Bros. merger isn’t truly about market share but rather whether he "can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN." 

Unfortunately for Ellison, much of the distrust is coming from inside the house. 

In a striking New York Times guest essay published on Tuesday, Ellison wrote that others have attempted to tell his story while he remained silent because the head of a news organization "shouldn’t put a finger on the scale," but he wouldn’t remain silent any longer. 

The essay quickly spread through CNN, where concerned staffers attempted to read between the lines to see if it offered a glimmer of hope. One CNN employee flatly rejected the notion that Ellison’s essay will ease tensions, while CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter called it "remarkable."

CNN STAFFERS SEE PARAMOUNT MERGER AS 'INEVITABLE' DESPITE LEGAL BATTLE DELAYING ELLISON TAKEOVER

Ellison’s Paramount is attempting to build a media empire of historic proportions by acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery for $111 billion. The European Union and the U.S. Justice Department have each signed off on the deal, with the final roadblocks coming from an antitrust lawsuit led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and a suit from the Writers Guild of America. Paramount recently agreed to delay the deal until next year while the lawsuits play out in court. 

"The states claim this deal will give one company too much influence over theatrical releases and cable operators, while the W.G.A. argues that our combined market power will hurt writers. Both suits imagine a Hollywood that no longer exists — an industry ruled by a handful of legacy studios," Ellison wrote.

Ellison noted that "a combined Paramount-Warner would account for less than 20 percent" of the time Americans spend watching television and "just 18 percent" of the domestic box office over the past 12 months.

"Those are not the numbers of a company that can dictate what audiences watch or what writers get paid," Ellison wrote. 

"I believe this fight is not really about market share," Ellison continued. "The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN. There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions."

CNN has been plagued with morale issues ahead of the looming merger, as the network has seen multiple leadership changes in recent memory and there is widespread concern about the direction of the network under Ellison. Some staffers are anxious about job security, while others are frightened that Bari Weiss, Ellison's handpicked editor-in-chief of CBS News who irks liberals throughout the media industry, would take on an oversight position at CNN. 

MOOD IS ‘HORRIFIC’ INSIDE CNN AS STAFFERS BRACE FOR CHANGE AMID POTENTIAL PARAMOUNT TAKEOVER, INSIDERS SAY

Ellison has previously publicly vowed that CNN will maintain its editorial independence, but skeptics don’t seem to take his promise at face value. Critics of Weiss and Ellison have accused them of bending the knee to Trump and trying to curry favor with his administration, but the high-powered mogul continues to insist that is not the case.  

"I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans; and when it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth," Ellison wrote.

"Great news organizations like CNN and CBS News are here to tell it straight down the middle," he added. "That requires newsrooms that reflect the whole world, not one side of it. And it requires independence."

Ellison wrote that CNN journalists would "continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve — not to any party or cause," once he takes control. 

PARAMOUNT-WBD MERGER ON HOLD AFTER JUDGE GRANTS TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER

Ellison, the son of billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, then noted that only 28 percent of Americans trust the news, citing a recent Gallup study. 

"The temptation is to say the problem lies elsewhere. Our obligation is to look inward and say: We can do better. We are in a moment when Americans trust few institutions, but journalists haven’t always helped their case by refusing to engage with critiques," Ellison wrote. "Trust can’t be argued back, but it can be earned back — story by story, day by day."

A veteran CNN staffer suggested that Ellison’s essay won’t exactly lift spirits. 

"I don't think it will calm the nerves of anyone at CNN! No one is worried about his politics, we're worried that he doesn't have any affection for the role of journalism," the staffer told Fox News Digital. 

"And as much as he paid lip service in this piece to those concerns, we don't really have to guess at what he'd do — his moves at CBS have reflected the opposite," they continued. "A disregard for independent storytelling, holding powerful people accountable, and investing in journalists and journalism, as executed by his hire, Bari Weiss."

CNN declined comment when reached by Fox News Digital. 

A former CNN producer, who isn't a fan of the direction the network has swung in recent years, doesn’t believe the essay will go over well with ex-colleagues. 

"David Ellison is making clear that under his leadership, CNN and CBS News must stop ‘refusing to engage’ with critics of their liberal bias and ‘look inward.’ He probably didn’t realize that he’s kicking a hornet’s nest," the ex-CNN producer said. 

"The folks at CNN and CBS News view any challenge to their biased, disconnected and badly produced programming as a violation of their free speech rights, and they’re coming at David and Bari with everything they’ve got," the source continued. "David is going to have to burn both places down before he can fix them."

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP 

CBS News did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Is this Trump’s last ‘last chance’? Ceaseless string of broken ceasefires fuels doubt over Iran deal
item.description: Trump calls diplomacy Iran's "last chance" after halting what he described as the biggest planned U.S. attack since World War II amid disputed talks.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump is warning Iran that it has one last chance to make a deal, even as Tehran denies the negotiations Trump says persuaded him to hold off on a major U.S. attack.

The clash has left the status of the diplomatic effort unclear. Trump says indirect talks could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and eventually address Iran’s nuclear program, while Tehran acknowledges only limited discussions with Oman and has not publicly embraced the broader deal Trump has described.

"There’s certainly an element of posturing involved," Ali Vaez, deputy program director for the Middle East at International Crisis Group, told Fox News Digital. "While there are no ‘talks’ in the sense of U.S. and Iranian officials sitting at the same venue exchanging proposals and counter-offers, engagement appears ongoing."

Trump said diplomacy persuaded him to call off a planned attack on Iran that he described as the biggest since World War II. Over the weekend, he said Iran and several Middle Eastern countries had asked for more time to finalize an agreement reopening Hormuz and addressing Tehran’s nuclear program.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN FIGHTING ISN'T OVER AS HE VOWS US WILL 'WIN' AS TALKS FADE

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said, however, that Tehran was neither holding talks with the United States nor expecting an American delegation. He described the Oman discussions as a bilateral effort to establish a temporary shipping corridor through the Strait.

Trump, in response, accused Iran’s leadership of being "unbelievably duplicitous."

"They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg,’ talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions," Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social.

Later that afternoon, Trump called the talks Iran’s "last chance" to avoid an escalation in U.S. strikes. He said negotiators would first seek to reopen the Strait, then turn to Tehran’s nuclear program.

"The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearization," Trump said in the Oval Office. "And that will take a little while."

Trump said reporters could learn more about the negotiations "today or tomorrow." Iran has not publicly endorsed either phase of his plan.

Saudi Arabia and other Gulf allies have urged Trump to hold off on the planned attack, fearing more Iranian reprisals against their territory. Jonathan Schanzer, executive director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said those concerns have complicated Trump’s next move.

"He’d like to be able to walk away with a win. The Iranians are not allowing him to do that," Schanzer told Fox News Digital. "There is not a clear path ahead for him at this moment."

US OFFICIAL SAYS JD VANCE MADE 'GREAT PROGRESS' IN IRAN TALKS, CALLS SNUB REPORTS 'FOREIGN PROPAGANDA'

A June memorandum also opened with promises of a broader settlement. The United States and Iran signed it to halt fighting, lift the U.S. blockade and reopen the Strait.

Shipping became the first test of the June memorandum, and it quickly exposed how far apart Washington and Tehran remained. Each side had its own plan for restoring commercial traffic through the Strait. When U.S. officials accused Iran of firing on commercial vessels days later, American strikes followed. Tehran said Washington had tried to force through a new shipping arrangement without its consent.

Negotiators never bridged that divide. Trump declared the ceasefire over in early July and expanded the U.S. air campaign. Iran answered with missile and drone attacks on American positions and regional partners.

That fighting set up another, shorter pause at the end of the month. Trump said mediators had asked the U.S. to hold fire, an arrangement Iran said it would match. Within days, Iranian missiles targeted U.S. forces in Jordan and the conflict spread again.

Brief breaks have become a feature of the conflict, which Schanzer described as a "ceasefire war."

"It is a war that is punctuated by short bouts of calm, only to see conflict return," Schanzer said.

Even if Oman succeeds in opening a temporary route, it would settle only the immediate question of how ships move through the Strait. Trump wants that step to lead into negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program, a sequence Tehran has yet to publicly embrace. "Fundamentally, both sides know that the status quo is a recipe for continued military and economic attrition without a clear endgame," Vaez said.

item.title: Reporter's Notebook: Inside the Senate showdown over Trump's push to scrap August recess
item.description: Trump wants the Senate to skip August recess until it passes the SAVE America Act requiring proof of citizenship to vote, but John Thune says no.
item.content:encoded:
"Should I stay or should I go now? If I go there will be trouble. And if I stay it will be double." – The Clash

The words "schedule" and "Congress" don’t always mesh.

But the formal Senate schedule has long had senators taking off at the end of this week until early September for the customary "August recess."

Only thing is, President Trump and some conservatives pushing for approval of the SAVE America Act don’t want the Senate to beg off. They assert that the Senate should remain in session until it passes the bill, which requires proof of citizenship to vote.

"I think there’s nothing more important than they pass the SAVE America Act. I think they should stay," said President Trump. "They do what they want. But I think they should stay."

SEN RICK SCOTT: AMERICANS WORK FIVE DAYS A WEEK, WHY CAN’T THE SENATE?

The Senate has already defeated two efforts to adopt the SAVE America Act. So there’s not an obvious pathway to alter those previous outcomes. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has rebuffed the President’s demands to stay in session.

"I don’t think having a Congress sitting around here for the month of August and quorum calls or having to vote on Democrat amendments is probably a good use of anybody's time," said Thune.

There’s tension between the South Dakota Republican and the President over the Senate’s legislative realities. Thune may be Majority Leader. But Thune believes the President bears responsibility for changing some minds on Capitol Hill.

"We have in the past suggested to he and his team to come up here and visit with some of my Republican colleagues," said Thune. "Now if he can change the facts and start moving some of those senators who are noes into yesses, then we have a different conversation. But that's just the reality."

As always, it’s about the math. And the SAVE America Act lacks the votes.

"I know Sen. Thune says the votes aren't there. I'm not saying he's wrong. I'm just saying people change their mind sometimes," argued Sen. John Kennedy, R-La.

But it doesn’t look like there will even be a vote on that, unless something ripens quickly.

That’s where Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah, Ted Cruz, R-Texas, Roger Marshall, R-Kas, Rick Scott, R-Fla., and others have suggested the Senate shouldn’t go on break unless they pass the bill.

So what happens next?

Let’s say we get to Friday night. The Senate has taken its final vote of the summer. Maybe to confirm Todd Blanche as Attorney General. Perhaps the measure named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., which sanctions Russia. The Senate is ready to finish until mid-September. In recent years, the Senate has not voted on a resolution to go out of session for weeks on end. That’s where SAVE America Act proponents would attempt to block such an effort. But its immaterial since there is no vote.

In the not too distant past, the House and Senate often approved "adjournment resolutions." But not right now. Such a plan must align with the wishes of the House of Representatives. Article I, Section 6 of the Constitution bars either body for adjourning for more than three days "without the Consent of the other." The House isn’t around to approve an adjournment resolution. It’s been out of session for a couple of weeks now. Moreover, it’s not clear that the House could adopt an adjournment resolution.

So, under the Constitution, each body must - at a minimum - hold a brief "pro forma" session where lawmakers convene for just a few seconds and then immediately gavel out. That meets the Constitutional requirement.

But there’s the rub.

When the Senate wraps up, Thune or one of his lieutenants would usually go to the floor and ask "unanimous consent" that the Senate meet on a series of Mondays and Thursdays or Tuesdays and Fridays between now and September. These are the "pro forma" sessions, convening at three-day intervals. But if Lee or someone wants to object, they’re stuck. The Senate can’t green light the set of pro formas. The Senate must have buy-in of all 100 senators.

REPUBLICAN SAYS TRUMP'S TOP ELECTION PRIORITY 'DEAD' IN SENATE AS GOP FRACTURES AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

But an objection in this case hardly blocks the recess or compels debate – let alone a vote or passage – on the SAVE America Act.

If Thune or his designee can’t get unanimous consent, the only option they have is to move to meet again the next day. Let’s say 9 a.m. ET. If someone objects to the time, it will meet at noon et under the Senate’s default protocols.

That said, this is where someone could force what might constitute the de facto "vote to go on recess." A Republican senator might demand a vote on the Senate adjourning for the day on Friday and meeting on Saturday. This is not a vote to "go on recess." But it’s the closest someone can engineer a possible vote related to Senate action.

A motion to adjourn is not debatable on the floor. But it is amendable. Someone could offer another option about when the Senate should meet. But that’s about it.

On this hypothetical Saturday session, it’s possible that Thune could simply get recognition and ask for the Senate to adjourn for the day again. One of those pushing the SAVE America Act doesn’t even get recognized to speak. However, if Thune is gracious and is willing to allow someone to have their say, they could get the floor and hold it as long as they want.

Note that doing so does not constitute a filibuster. Filibusters are efforts by senators to stop something. In this case, advocates of the SAVE America Act are trying to start something. So no filibuster. This would just be a really long speech. But Thune might not let it come to that. And even though they’ve chattered about it a lot, the strongest advocates of the SAVE America Act have not taken advantage of their prerogatives as senators and gone down to hold the floor at length.

Keep in mind that SAVE America Act advocates could potentially do this and push for recognition on the floor on all subsequent days during the August recess. Thune could block them from speaking because the order of the day is to convene and adjourn during a pro forma session. And if the SAVE America Act faction were to push for a vote, all it takes is another senator to block them on the floor.

One might ask the question about whether the SAVE America Act group might demand a "live" quorum call (where all senators must report to the floor for attendance) or even the more extreme motion of "instructing the Sergeant at Arms to arrest" absent senators and bring them to the floor. Well, this works at cross purposes during August. The reason? The Senate doesn’t have a quorum. In the old days, the Senate took quorum calls to establish if enough senators present were present to do business. It violates the Constitution to conduct business without a quorum present.

The SAVE America Act coalition may prove that there aren’t enough senators in Washington to conduct business. That helps make their point. But it also forces the Senate to adjourn because it can’t operate without a quorum.

WATCH: DEMOCRATS ADMIT WHEN THEY'D ELIMINATE THE FILIBUSTER AS SAVE ACT FIGHT HEATS UP

These gambits might not achieve the legislative goal of passing the SAVE America Act. But there are other benefits for SAVE America Act advocates. A series of lengthy speeches could potentially delay the recess. These Republican senators could argue that they are willing to stay and debate the SAVE America Act while their colleagues fled Washington for summer. Such a maneuver would focus attention on the issue. It would draw a contrast between senators willing to fight for the issue and those who went home. The effort might impress President Trump. And such a maneuver could show divides between them and Thune – who the President often chastises.

But pass the SAVE America Act? It’s not going to do that. And some Republican senators emphasize the importance of taking a few weeks off so their colleagues can campaign.

"The worst case scenario is for us is to stay all the way through and then we lose the Senate in the days ahead," said Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., on Fox. "Then President Trump is dealing with all the impeachment crazy all over again."

Remaining in Washington for the next five weeks would pull the most vulnerable GOP senator off the trail, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine.

Collins was crystal clear when pressed by yours truly whether she would campaign and miss her first roll call vote since entering the Senate in 1997.

"I don’t miss votes," said an emphatic Collins.

So don’t expect the Senate to forgo the recess at the end of the week.

In fact, a decision by the Senate to go on recess may even work to the political advantage of those pushing for the SAVE America Act. They can then rail against Thune’s leadership and their colleagues for not passing the bill. Again, they don’t score the legislative outcome. But they sure rack up some political points.

This is why those philosopher kings who comprise the band The Clash may have been on to something. If the Senate stays, Republicans can’t pass the SAVE America Act. But if they go, certain GOP senators can rabble rouse.

There’s trouble whether senators stay or go.

item.title: Chicago White Sox lead American League Central but face a red-hot Boston Red Sox team Tuesday
item.description: The Boston Red Sox ride a stunning 28-5 surge and the Adley Rutschman acquisition into a pivotal matchup with the AL Central-leading White Sox.
item.content:encoded:
With the trade deadline passing Monday, we are officially on playoff watch for teams. Every game from here on will take on a bit more intensity and importance. We know a few teams have dropped out of the race after the trades that took place. Others bolstered their roster, and we have two of them that are going all in, taking each other on today as the White Sox face the Red Sox.

It is the start of August, and the Chicago White Sox are leading the American League Central. Now, before you put a reservation down for some playoff tickets, keep in mind that the Tigers were leading the division to start August last year, and they were heavy favorites to win it. The problem is that the Guardians were lurking, had a spectacular September, and took down the AL Central. The Tigers still made the postseason, but it feels like we will get two Wild Card teams from the American League East, so the safest path for the White Sox is to win the division.

They did add to the team at the trade deadline, and that should instill a bit more confidence in the roster. Their rotation will now have a couple of dependable guys. Davis Martin is one of those guys, but he is approaching the most innings he's pitched in a year. He is 9-5 with a 3.62 ERA and a 1.26 WHIP. He struggled in July after a mixed bag of results in June, so you do need to wonder if his success is fading. The White Sox went 1-4 in his starts in July, and he allowed 16 earned runs in 24 innings. One of those games was against the Red Sox where he allowed five earned runs in four innings.

RED SOX COME BACK FROM THE DEAD, MOVE INTO POSTSEASON CONTENTION WITH REMARKABLE 14-GAME WIN STREAK

The Boston Red Sox made arguably the most shocking move of the trade deadline, by acquiring Adley Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24. Since that point, they've gone 28-5. They have had three separate five-game or more winning streaks in that stretch, including one they are on right now. They just swept the Dodgers, arguably the best team in baseball. Can this level of winning be sustained for two more months? Unlikely, but it is impressive nonetheless.

Tuesday they send Patrick Sandoval to the hill in hopes of making it six games in a row. For the year, Sandoval only has four starts under his belt and carries a 3.32 ERA and a 1.58 WHIP. None of his starts have been ugly or bad by any means. He did allow four earned runs against the Rays, but the other three saw him allow two or fewer. He faced the White Sox in the first start of his season and went 4.1 innings and allowed just one earned run on five hits.

It is hard to pick against the Red Sox with how hot as they've been. I have faded them in a couple of spots, but it didn't work out. The additions from the deadline should rejuvenate both of these teams as well. I think we should take the hotter team today, and I think we also need to start fading Martin. He will probably still have some good starts left, but he has struggled lately. He also didn't have a great June. His arm might just be getting tired. I'll take Sandoval and the Red Sox on the moneyline tonight.

item.title: Dave Rubin warns Trump has less than 3 months to push agenda before midterm elections
item.description: Dave Rubin warns that if Republicans lose the House in midterm elections, Trump faces impeachment and the MAGA movement faces an existential threat.
item.content:encoded:
Despite having two and a half years left in office, President Donald Trump may have only three months to effectively implement his agenda, podcaster Dave Rubin said on Tuesday's episode of "Hang Out with Sean Hannity."

Rubin said Trump is likely to face hurdles beyond the typical challenges of policymaking if Democrats gain ground in Congress as a result of this year's midterm elections.

"If [Republicans] lose the House, [President Trump] is going to get hung up in impeachment," Rubin said.

100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY

"He'll be impeached, but he probably won't be removed from office. They're not going to get enough votes in the Senate one way or another."

Still, Rubin contended, the Make America Great Again movement faces an existential threat as its leader's time in the Oval Office draws to a close.

"The point is that the process to end these last 10 years of MAGA and everything that has happened since 2015 will begin," he said.

The emboldening of the "crazies on the left" isn't the only threat, he added. Infighting among conservatives is going to "go completely bananas."

GOP CIVIL WAR ERUPTS OVER TRUMP'S LATEST AGENDA PUSH AS KEY REPUBLICANS THREATEN TO SINK MEGABILL

"It's going to be like rats jumping from a ship, and then you're going to have all these people leaving Trump and trying to pick up the pieces. It's going to be complete chaos."

Meanwhile, in Washington, D.C., Republicans are sounding the alarm that Trump’s demand to cancel the August recess could cost the GOP seats in the midterms, as vulnerable incumbents say they need to be home campaigning and connecting with constituents, not stuck on Capitol Hill.

"The Rubin Report" host acknowledged it was clichéd to claim the upcoming midterms would be "the most important election of all time," but said he does not see "how it could possibly be more important than it is right now."

"We are on the edge of handing the keys to the castle to people who are telling us they want to burn the castle down."

Fox News Digital's Alex Miller contributed to this report.

item.title: Battlefield robots open new front in innovation war with major US adversary
item.description: EdgeRunner AI's onboard neural network lets military robots continue missions after losing connectivity, eliminating reliance on Starlink or cloud.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: The U.S. Army is teaming up with an artificial intelligence (AI) company to build an AI "brain" for military robots that can think, understand their surroundings and continue missions even after losing contact with human operators as the race for AI dominance intensifies.

Working with the Army Research Laboratory, defense AI company EdgeRunner AI has developed an onboard AI system that allows military robots to function in the battlefield without relying on cloud computing or an internet connection in environments where connectivity is lost.

"We like to think of robots as the next frontier of AI," EdgeRunner AI founder and CEO Tyler Saltsman told Fox News Digital.

"Think of them as a very far-out edge device, kind of like a cell phone, a tablet or a laptop. But now what we can do is we can put a brain, or a neural network, right on that robot so that robots can have context when they're on a mission helping the warfighter."

CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE

The partnership comes as the U.S. and China race to integrate AI into their militaries, with both countries viewing AI as critical to maintaining a technological edge in future conflicts.

Saltsman said it's important for the U.S. to stay ahead in the global AI race, calling China's dominance in drone manufacturing "problematic."

"Whether or not China's ahead of us is debatable, but if China is, it's not by much," he said.

Saltsman said today's AI is "too generalized," which is why his company is developing technology built for specific military missions.

"Warfighters don't need 19th-century poetry," he said. "They need specific intelligence to his or her occupation in order to make better decisions in the heat of battle and that can increase the probability of winning the fight."

Working alongside aerial drones, the AI is designed to help robots "problem solve through different routes" while detecting explosives, carrying ammunition, scouting routes and reporting enemy activity.

UKRAINE’S BATTLEFIELD IS TRANSFORMING THE FUTURE OF NATO

"As you combine them together, you get a much better clarity of the battlefield and increased situational awareness," he said.

When communications are cut off, Saltsman said the military will need autonomous systems that can continue making decisions on their own.

"You can have a human pilot that controls the ground robot or the drone in the air," he said. "But then if they were to be jammed by a radar jammer and lose connectivity, then the neural network on that robot can still continue the mission and still aid the warfighter."

Saltsman argued the military "can't rely on internet access in war," warning that depending on systems like SpaceX's Starlink could add a "risk" to missions.

"The problem with Starlink is if you use it, you're effectively showing the enemy where you are, so you might as well be wearing a beacon on you saying, 'Hey, here's where I'm located,'" he said.

INSIDE CHINA’S AI ‘WOLF PACK’ DRONES BUILT WITH TAIWAN CONFLICT IN MIND

Pointing to the Russia-Ukraine war, Saltsman said the success of drones has sparked a new push for autonomous ground robots.

"As drones have become ubiquitous, now ground robots are like the next thing and then eventually humanoid robots so robots that move and look like humans," he said.

Despite the push to advance military AI, Saltsman said safety can't take a back seat and that the technology is built using "transparent" datasets to "understand the biases" of the AI.

"That's another thing that differentiates us," he said. "One of the problems is how to use AI safely, how to put guardrails around it and how to understand it."

While the technology remains in the "development phase," Saltsman said the breakthrough gives robots the ability to understand what they see, not just detect it.

"You can put computer vision models on robots so they can see, but if they don't understand the context of what they're seeing, they're not useful and that's what we're solving for."

item.title: Post-trade deadline futures bets worth taking on the World Series and division winners
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers remain World Series favorites at +160, but the Chicago Cubs at 15:1 and the Padres at +7500 could offer serious value.
item.content:encoded:
The trade deadline is now behind us, and we had a flurry of deals yesterday. As a sports bettor, it is important to pay attention to this information. Not only does it signify that some teams are going to start (or further continue) tanking. It also means we probably need to reevaluate the teams and even some of our future positions. I don't normally look at a ton of baseball futures because it takes too long for them to pay off, but there might be some opportunity for us to grab value on some bets before the season ends.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are still the overwhelming favorites to win the World Series. They are +160 to win it now. Can you imagine having to face Tarik Skubal, then Yoshinobu Yamamoto, then Blake Snell, then Tyler Glasnow, then Shohei Ohtani as a rotation in a seven-game series? It is rather absurd. However, there is no value remaining at +160. The Red Sox were major players at the deadline, but they didn't get much better in their rotation. I just don't see the pitching to get it done. The Chicago Cubs at 15:1 might actually have what it takes to get past the Dodgers. They just so happen to play each other tonight, with Skubal's debut coming. The Cubs added Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes to their rotation, and that should - as long as they don't suffer more injuries - give them solid enough pitching to navigate a lot of series. Another National League team that I like is the Padres at +7500.

The Padres did not fold as some people expected. Instead, they went out and addressed their starting pitching needs. They were able to get Robbie Ray (a former Cy Young winner), and they also grabbed Casey Mize from the Tigers. Their hitting has been down, but you would think some of their guys will come back to their normal averages. At this value, I think you have to take them. The Phillies at +1800 added a guy in Luis Arraez who will be on base, and Zack Wheeler and Christopher Sanchez give them a chance against anyone.

In the American League, I like the Mariners, who addressed their biggest need by acquiring Taylor Ward from the Orioles. They are at +2200 and should have the best rotation in the playoffs, but they need to make it there first. The Rays are +1300 and one of the best teams in baseball. They will have a great 1-2 punch in Shane McClanahan and Freddy Peralta.

Fellow writer, Geoff Clark, took the Angels to be the worst team in baseball this season before the year began. He got them at +2200, so he has excellent value. They are now +145 to have the fewest wins, and they have two fewer than anyone in baseball. They traded away a lot of guys, kept their young talent, and acquired guys that could actually help later. I think even at +145 you're looking at a good ticket. The only issue is that the Angels play in the worst division in baseball while the Rockies play in one of the better ones. The Athletics have just two more wins than the Angels and are also tanking. Assuming both play their division down the stretch, the Rockies (+135) could lose more games.

item.title: Trump's AG pick survives — for now — as Republicans question if White House deal will hold
item.description: Todd Blanche's committee vote hinged on a deal with Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, but Senate Republicans remain divided on his path to confirmation.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the Justice Department survived a crucial hurdle on Tuesday after reaching an agreement with key holdouts, but whether he reaches the finish line remains an open question.

The Senate Judiciary Committee, after last-minute delays and drama, confirmed acting Attorney General Todd Blanche in a 12-10 vote, sending him to the Senate floor for his final test. His success on committee remained in the air until the weekend, when a deal to win over Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, was announced.

And the duo accepted the terms of the deal, which would permanently rescind the nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund and narrow the scope of Trump and his family’s audit immunity — two major components of his settlement with the IRS that Blanche rolled out earlier this year.

TRUMP'S AG PICK OFF LIFE SUPPORT AFTER KEY REPUBLICAN REBELS RELENT

Some lawmakers, however, are questioning the agreement and whether Trump will actually comply.

Tillis said of the anti-weaponization fund that, "we've got enough data in the record to know it's rescinded." But he acknowledged that, "Other people are asking about the audit component, but it's another area where I put a lot of faith in John Cornyn."

"I think that he believes that we're at a place where it's narrowly defined, and it would be very difficult for anybody to construe it as some sort of get out of audit free — for any kind of future — I know it's retrospective, it is not prospective," Cornyn said.

"And I believe that only the parties to the agreement may be in a position to be exempted. So, that's, you know, that's enough for me," he continued.

DOJ BARS IRS FROM AUDITING TRUMP’S PRIOR TAX RETURNS IN SETTLEMENT ORDER SIGNED BY BLANCHE

The duo’s colleagues on the Senate Judiciary Committee have a divided outlook on the nature of the deal, given Trump’s desire to revive the fund and because the audit immunity wasn’t fully buried.

"Cornyn and Tillis seem to have gotten nothing meaningful," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital. "You know, the tax immunity deal is still unlimited, in terms of past potential liability. And the slush fund — the thug fund as I call it — is still alive and well, so far as Donald Trump is concerned. And he's the one who counts."

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Fox News Digital Trump "could renege on their agreement."

"I'm not saying he will or he won't, what’s stopping the president from doing anything? But it was important to Cornyn and important to Tillis," Kennedy said. "And I'm glad they got cooperation from, finally, from DOJ. And I think I've heard some other senators who have grumbled a little bit about not voting for Blanche, but I think they will. He'll be confirmed."

To Kennedy’s latter point, Blanche’s trajectory to becoming the permanent attorney general still isn’t guaranteed.

A handful of Senate Republicans are not outright declaring their support for his nomination. And as usual, that turns into a math problem on the Senate floor.

TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS

Right now, Blanche can only afford to lose two votes on the floor. That’s because Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., is still missing in action while he recovers from a fall at his Washington, D.C., home in June.

And the numbers look tough going forward. Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, Susan Collins, R-Maine, John Curtis, R-Utah, and Bill Cassidy, R-La., are still on the fence about Blanche.

Murkowski told reporters that she wants "to find out a little bit more about the negotiations," over the weekend that led to the deal.

"I think certainly the fact that he has signed this order, basically disbanding [the fund] — that’s a pretty good step," Murkowski said.

Meanwhile, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., wants to get rolling on the Blanche confirmation as soon as possible, given the laundry list of to-do items he and Republicans are trying to check off before leaving Washington, D.C., for a break until September.

Because of the schedule and outlying variables, he couldn’t guarantee that Blanche’s confirmation would get done before September.

"Ideally, we'd like to get him done, and particularly if he comes out, which looks like he now will, affirmatively out of the committee," Thune said. "Then I'd like to figure out a way, a path forward to get him done."

item.title: Bomb-thrower Dem makes shocking promise to kick Schumer to curb during Senate debate
item.description: Seth Moulton vowed not to support Chuck Schumer as Senate leader, intensifying a Democratic Party clash between younger candidates and establishment.
item.content:encoded:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., could be facing headwinds in his quest for power even if Democrats win back Congress' upper chamber in November.

Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., who is running in a heated primary against incumbent Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., said during a debate Monday night that he would not support Schumer as leader if elected.

"The first vote that I take when I get to the United States Senate will be for not Senator Schumer, because we need new leadership at the top as well," Moulton said.

MASSACHUSETTS SENATE CANDIDATES TRADE SHARP ATTACKS IN FIERY DEBATE AS INCUMBENT MARKEY SKIPS EVENT

He was alluding to the selection of each party's leadership ranks, which generally comes after the November election.

Markey also did not explicitly endorse Schumer for leader, but he has supported him in the past. Markey’s campaign directed Fox News Digital to the senator’s comments during the debate when asked about his support for Schumer.

"We need a big debate about new leadership in the Senate – the direction of the Senate," Markey said.

It's a notable move for both Democrats to distance themselves from the current party leader, as the primary for Massachusetts' Senate seat has been marked by bitter accusations on both sides.

Moulton has accused Markey of selling out his beliefs by taking money from fossil fuel groups, and slammed the 80-year-old senator for his age and lengthy tenure in Congress. Meanwhile, Markey has attacked Moulton for investing in defense companies that the House committees he sits on have jurisdiction over, and his prior comments on transgender participation in youth sports.

The Salem-area House Democrat has a notable history of challenging his party's leadership. In 2018, he led a rebellion within his caucus to challenge former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., from keeping her leadership post.

He said in a 2019 HuffPost interview that Democratic leadership was "failing" in standing up to President Donald Trump and accused leaders of fueling divisions within the caucus.

Now that fight is playing out in deep blue Massachusetts as part of a wider national war within the Democratic Party. Younger candidates are challenging the establishment left in races across the U.S., arguing that the status quo is not working for Americans today.

HOUSE PROGRESSIVES REVIVE GREEN NEW DEAL FOR PUBLIC SCHOOLS AS DEM CIVIL WAR EMPOWERS FAR LEFT

"If you think the Democratic establishment is winning for Massachusetts, if you think it's fine that the Democratic establishment has allowed a second term of Donald Trump, then vote for the status quo," Moulton said during the debate.

Schumer is not up for re-election until 2028, but he must face his fellow Senate Democrats every two years in the internal leadership race to make a case for why he should stay at the helm.

And younger candidates like Moulton could pose issues for him on that front.

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., who at 53 years old is younger than a significant number of his colleagues, was evasive when asked if Schumer should remain in leadership during an interview on CNN's "State of the Union" in March.

SCHUMER DODGES QUESTION ON WHETHER DSA BELONGS IN DEMOCRATIC PARTY

"Well, I think we are united right now as a caucus. There’s always a lot of focus on Senator Schumer and [House Minority] Leader Jeffries," Murphy said when asked if he supported Schumer, who he said had a "tough job."

Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic socialist running in the Michigan Senate primary against an opponent backed by the New York Democrat, said at a recent rally, "If you're Chuck Schumer, I'm pretty damn dangerous."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

And Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., has also called on Schumer to step aside and make way for new leadership.

Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer's office and Markey's campaign for comment on Moulton's remarks.

item.title: Ted Cruz urges Senate to stay in Washington until Protect College Sports Act passes this week
item.description: President Donald Trump says he's hopeful for a Senate floor vote on the "Protect College Sports Act," but political hurdles could push action into September.
item.content:encoded:
After the Big Ten and SEC agreed to throw their support behind the "Protect College Sports Act" during an intense negotiating period last week, congressional leaders have finally released final text language around the legislation.

On Monday, while meeting with reporters in the Oval Office, President Donald Trump mentioned that he was hopeful that a vote would finally take place on the Senate floor regarding the legislation that has led to plenty of contentious moments behind the scenes.

The bipartisan bill, which was first introduced by Senators Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., along with Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., has been the talk of college athletics over the past week, which comes on the heels of a strenuous stretch of negotiations.

LAWMAKERS PRAISE BIPARTISAN EFFORTS LED BY TRUMP ADMIN TO ‘PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS FOR FUTURE GENERATIONS’

While other conferences across the country had put their support behind the legislation that had yet to be finalized, the SEC and Big Ten wanted to see concessions made that would garner their approval.

After pushing for their support and pointing toward this week as when the legislation could be voted on, having this move into the month of September could end up generating a lane in which this might not be passed at all, with congressional leaders focused on midterms and other important matters for the country.

RUNNING OUT OF TIME: SEC, BIG TEN WAIT ON 'PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT' REVISIONS AS AUGUST RECESS NEARS

That is obviously not in the best interest of those involved in this process, given the amount of work that has gone into putting this bill together.

Last Friday, after a nudge from the White House, senators finally received the support of the two biggest conferences in college sports. But even then, those involved had not seen a final bill, rather given a walkthrough from those involved around Capitol Hill.

By the close of business on Monday night, and early Tuesday morning, Thune did not start the cloture procedure, and the likelihood of this getting to a vote by Friday dwindles by the day for this week.

On a call with a group of reporters Monday afternoon, a Senate Commerce Committee aide mentioned that there were political hurdles in getting this to a vote before Congress takes their August recess later in the week.

Some of those other priorities for the Senate included Russia sanctions, confirmation of nominations and the CLARITY Act among others.

But, Cruz was still persistent in his message that the Senate should stay in Washington until this was passed. There are also other issues that should certainly take precedent over a college sports bill, like the ongoing fires in Spokane, where Cantwell was rightfully attending to over the weekend.

According to language in the bill, which could still be tweaked, obtained by Fox News Digital/OutKick, there were a number of changes made compared to the first version.

An athletic department is not going to wait around until after the season ends to announce/or hire their new coach. And, if this were to be brought before a court, a coach would have a good argument that the government is hindering their ability to obtain work.

As for what is next, that depends on how quick this can be brought for cloture.

A number of sources have mentioned that getting this voted on by Friday evening will be a tall task. But, that doesn’t mean Senators are not going to try.

Given the amount of rebuttal this could receive from Senators who are not in favor of the 'Protect College Sports Act', like Sen. Tommy Tuberville and others, this process could drag into September when Congress returns from recess.

item.title: Ceuta migrant surge exposes Spain-Morocco tensions as Islamist groups reportedly seek to exploit border crisis
item.description: Spain reports 72 deaths as the Ceuta migrant crisis deepens, with intelligence officials saying Morocco allowed border controls to gradually relax.
item.content:encoded:
Thousands of migrants remained stranded in Spain’s North African city of Ceuta on Tuesday as the European Union offered emergency assistance to reinforce the enclave’s border and Spanish authorities investigated whether criminals or suspected jihadists used last week’s chaotic mass crossing to enter European territory.

Approximately 72,000 people entered Ceuta from Morocco, and about 70,000 have since returned, Spanish officials said Tuesday, leaving roughly 2,000 people in the small territory. Reception facilities remained overwhelmed as authorities struggled to shelter hundreds of migrant minors and determine the status of those who remained.

Local authorities were processing 862 migrant minors, who receive special protections under Spanish law and cannot be summarily returned. The Associated Press reported that children were begging for food or sleeping outside after the youth shelter became overwhelmed.

SPAIN DEPLOYS MILITARY AFTER THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS OVERWHELM BORDER ENCLAVE, AT LEAST 18 DEAD

The EU offered Spain assistance, including emergency financial support, to strengthen protection of its external border in Ceuta, European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner said Tuesday following an emergency meeting of the bloc’s ministers in Brussels.

Brunner said the unprecedented crossing was fueled by criminal smuggling networks and disinformation spread through social media, as Spanish authorities were examining whether known criminals or suspected jihadists exploited the scale and disorder of the crossing to enter Ceuta undetected.

Spain’s National Police and Guardia Civil were reviewing video of the crossings and checking people who remained in the territory against criminal and counterterrorism databases, according to El Confidencial, which cited Spanish Interior Ministry sources.

The Spanish outlet reported that authorities were searching for known criminals and possible jihadists who may have entered among the tens of thousands who crossed. Interior Ministry sources acknowledged that the sheer scale of the surge created a genuine infiltration risk, according to the report.

El Confidencial said the concern was heightened by Ceuta’s proximity to Fnideq, also known as Castillejos, a Moroccan border town that has figured in previous jihadist recruitment investigations. Authorities have previously dismantled extremist cells operating across the Ceuta-Fnideq border area, while hundreds of people from northern Morocco traveled to join ISIS and other terrorist groups in Syria and Iraq during the mid-2010s, the outlet reported.

TRUMP BLASTS SPAIN MIGRANT SURGE AS 'CATASTROPHE,' WARNS US COULD FACE WORSE IF DEMOCRATS REGAIN POWER

The crisis is also creating an opening for Islamist movements seeking to weaken confidence in Morocco’s government, according to Zineb Riboua, a research fellow at the Hudson Institute.

Riboua said in an article that Moroccan Islamists have spent years portraying the monarchy as overly secular and pro-Western, attacking its relationships with the United States and Israel and encouraging the belief that young Moroccans have little future at home.

At the same time, she wrote, Islamist voices have promoted an idealized image of Europe as a place where prosperity and legal status can be easily obtained.

Riboua said the Ceuta crisis allows those movements to transform public frustration over migration, unemployment and economic conditions into a broader political attack on the Moroccan state ahead of the national elections in September.

Evidence has separately emerged that the mass crossing was preceded by an extensive online mobilization campaign.

An open-source intelligence report prepared by Golden Owl Intelligence traced weeks of activity across TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, including misleading interpretations of Spanish immigration law and practical information about routes, meeting points and recommended crossing times.

The report estimated that the content generated more than 11 million potential impressions through posts, videos, comments and interactions. It also identified messaging groups administered through telephone numbers carrying Algerian international codes.

The campaign accelerated after Spain’s Supreme Court issued a July 8 ruling concerning the immediate return of migrants intercepted at sea near Ceuta and Melilla, according to the report. Simplified and misleading interpretations of the decision, combined with confusion surrounding Spain’s policy to regularize hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants, were presented online as evidence that people who reached Spanish territory would be allowed to remain and eventually obtain legal status.

The investigation documented the later circulation of maps, swimming routes, transportation information and suggested departure points as tens of thousands of people began moving toward the border.

MIGRANT CRISIS PUSHES ITALY TO RESTORE BORDER CHECKS WITH SPAIN, TESTING EUROPE'S OPEN-BORDER SYSTEM

Morocco’s Interior Ministry spokesman Rachid El Khalfi said at a news conference Sunday that the surge resulted from several overlapping factors, including the exploitation of digital platforms, misleading information, human-trafficking networks and inaccurate interpretations of legal and administrative developments.

Khalfi said the messaging created the false impression that the border was open and that people could reach European territory without legal consequences. He said Moroccan prosecutors had opened investigations to identify those responsible and determine the appropriate legal consequences.

Reuters and the Associated Press have independently documented cases in which online claims influenced people to travel toward Ceuta. Reuters interviewed a Moroccan teenager who said Instagram videos inspired him and his cousin to make the journey, while a Moroccan human-rights activist told the AP that social-media posts initially claimed the border was open and later promoted a misleading interpretation of the Supreme Court ruling.

The crisis has also placed Spain’s intelligence services and its relationship with Morocco under scrutiny.

El País and Cadena SER reported, citing officials familiar with Spain’s intelligence assessment, that Morocco did not plan the mass crossing but allowed it to unfold after border controls were gradually relaxed.

Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said Spain’s foreign intelligence agency had not warned him of an imminent surge of that magnitude.

WHITE HOUSE BLASTS SPANISH GOVERNMENT AS THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS SURGE FROM MOROCCO, EMERGENCY REQUEST DENIED

Morocco has denied deliberately orchestrating the crossing. Interior Ministry spokesman Rachid Khalfi blamed the surge on online misinformation, human-trafficking networks and distorted interpretations of Spanish legal and administrative developments, according to The Jerusalem Post. The ministry said Morocco remained committed to international cooperation against irregular migration and human trafficking.

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares defended Rabat’s response, saying Moroccan authorities quickly provided police support and helped facilitate the return of most of those who crossed.

Juan Jesus Vivas Lara, president of the autonomous city of Ceuta, offered a sharply different assessment, telling El País that many Ceuta residents believed Morocco had allowed, if not orchestrated, the surge.

"Morocco has shown us that it isn’t reliable," Vivas said. "There’s no alternative but to put in place whatever means are necessary to ensure it cannot do this again."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Moroccan government for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: DOJ charges 19 defendants in alleged $4M Philadelphia Medicare and Medicaid fraud
item.description: The Department of Justice expanded its Northeast Health Care Fraud Strike Force to Philadelphia, charging 19 defendants in alleged Medicare and Medicaid schemes.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: The Justice Department announced Tuesday that it is expanding its Northeast Health Care Fraud Strike Force to Philadelphia as federal and state authorities target alleged Medicare and Medicaid fraud involving home health care services.

The expansion will establish a strike force office in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania and bring together the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the district.

In connection with the announcement, federal and Pennsylvania authorities charged 19 defendants accused of participating in schemes involving more than $4 million in claims submitted to Medicare and Medicaid, according to a DOJ release obtained by Fox News. The defendants include home health care company owners, employees, purported aides and Medicaid recipients.

Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday also announced a plea agreement involving the final defendant in a previously charged 21-defendant case tied to more than $1.7 million in claims.

LETITIA JAMES HAMMERED AFTER NY MEDICAID FRAUD UNIT FUNDING FROZEN OVER INEFFECTIVE ENFORCEMENT

"The Fraud Division’s expansion into the Eastern District of Pennsylvania brings enhanced federal resources to a district with an established tradition of strong health care fraud enforcement," the DOJ said. "The partnership between the Fraud Division and the Eastern District of Pennsylvania will uniquely enable law enforcement to combat criminals who hide behind corporations to commit fraud."

The cases include allegations that home health aides billed Medicaid for services while they were incarcerated, hospitalized, working other jobs or traveling overseas. In another case, prosecutors said a Medicaid recipient claimed to require extensive home health assistance while also working as a carpenter.

Other defendants allegedly submitted overlapping or impossible work hours, including claims exceeding 24 hours of care in a single day, according to the release. One home health care agency and its owners were also charged with allegedly billing Medicaid for false clock-ins and clock-outs.

DOJ CHARGES 10 SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA DEFENDANTS IN LARGEST FEDERAL HEALTHCARE FRAUD CRACKDOWN IN US HISTORY

"The Strike Force’s expansion makes clear that the Fraud Division will use every available legal tool to identify, investigate, and prosecute offenses against the American people," the DOJ said.

The Philadelphia office will work with the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, the FBI, the DEA and other law enforcement agencies.

The DOJ said the expansion follows recent additions to the strike force program in California, Arizona, Nevada, Massachusetts and Minnesota, as well as two national health care fraud enforcement actions involving more than $15 billion in alleged losses in 2025 and more than $6 billion in alleged losses in 2026.

item.title: NBA great says he nearly 'dropped dead' due to blood clot as he offers advice to Victor Wembanyama
item.description: Chris Bosh warns Victor Wembanyama about deep vein thrombosis after his own near-death pulmonary embolism forced him into early NBA retirement.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Bosh wants to spread awareness of blood clots after he nearly "dropped dead" earlier this year.

Back in February, Bosh, who was forced to retire because of his history of blood clots, said that he woke up "covered" in his own blood. He recently revealed that he suffered from a pulmonary embolism.

A pulmonary embolism normally occurs when a blood clot breaks loose and travels to the lungs.
